candidato.titulo: Malaria antibody protects infants but lowers immune response to R21 vaccine, trial finds
candidato.resumo: A single intramuscular dose of an experimental malaria monoclonal antibody safely provided infants with strong protection during Mali's six-month malaria season. However, potential interference with the R21 malaria vaccine is putting plans to pursue development of L9LS for this age group on hold, according to results from a clinical trial presented at the annual meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (ASTMH).

texto_fonte:
Malaria antibody protects infants but lowers immune response to R21 vaccine, trial finds
A single intramuscular dose of an experimental malaria monoclonal antibody safely provided infants with strong protection during Mali's six-month malaria season. However, potential interference with the R21 malaria vaccine is putting plans to pursue development of L9LS for this age group on hold, according to results from a clinical trial presented at the annual meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (ASTMH).
The Phase Ib trial involved a monoclonal antibody known as L9LS that was developed by the U.S. National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID). The antibody has a strong track record of safety and efficacy in clinical trials involving older children in Mali and Kenya.
"We wanted to test L9LS in infants as young as 1 month old, because children are not eligible for malaria vaccination until they are at least 5 months old—and that leaves them especially vulnerable, particularly during times of intense malaria transmission," said Kassoum Kayentao, a physician-scientist at the University of Sciences, Techniques and Technologies in Bamako, Mali, which conducted the trial in partnership with NIAID colleagues.
"While protective efficacy against malaria infection was 78%, the monoclonal antibody also appeared to interfere with the immune response to subsequent immunization with the R21 malaria vaccine, which is widely used in Mali. That means we must pause our plans to conduct a larger trial with infants."
Researchers said they will continue exploring the potential of L9LS to reduce the burden of malaria in children who remain at risk of malaria after completing the R21 vaccine series, since the vaccine does not provide complete and long-lasting protection. For example, L9LS may be used for post-discharge prophylaxis in hospitalized children with severe malaria or anemia, or as an alternative to seasonal malaria chemoprevention following vaccination.
Kayentao said there is also interest in considering L9LS for pregnant women given the significant morbidity and mortality associated with malaria during pregnancy.
Despite setback with infants, L9LS continues to show strong protective efficacy
Malaria monoclonal antibodies, or "mAbs," are naturally occurring proteins isolated from human immune cells in the laboratory and then manufactured in large quantities. These mAbs are intended to provide nearly immediate protection that lasts for about six months. There is considerable interest in deploying them in the fight against malaria.
According to the World Health Organization, about 610,000 people died from malaria in 2024, most of them young African children. That toll has barely budged in the last 10 years, possibly due in part to a rise in antimalarial drug and insecticide resistance.
L9LS is the most advanced malaria mAb in the pipeline. In previous trials involving infants and older children in Mali and Kenya, a single subcutaneous injection of L9LS—meaning it was injected into tissue just beneath the skin—proved highly efficacious in preventing malaria illness.
The results from the latest Mali trial were presented at the ASTMH annual meeting by lead author Dr. Bickey Chang, a clinical fellow at NIAID. The trial, which was conducted in 2024 and 2025 at three sites in Mali, enrolled 180 healthy children ages 1–12 months. Half received L9LS, which was delivered via an intramuscular injection. (Compared with a subcutaneous injection, this route of administration can speed absorption of a medication by injecting it deep into muscle tissue.) The other half received a placebo injection of sterile salt water.
L9LS was safe and well tolerated by those who received it and provided protective efficacy of 78% against infection with the Plasmodium falciparum malaria parasite, the deadliest of the Plasmodium species that infect humans and the most prevalent one in Africa.
But the researchers also observed that a key antibody response generated by the R21 vaccine was about 20% to 30% lower in study participants who received L9LS five months before receiving the vaccine, compared with those who had received a placebo.
This mAb-vaccine interaction may be due to the fact that L9LS binds weakly to the malaria protein contained in the R21 vaccine, even though that protein is not the primary target of L9LS.
Further clinical development of L9LS for children who have not completed the three-dose R21 vaccine series—those less than 2 to 3 years of age—will not be considered until researchers can determine whether the observed reduction in antibody production actually compromises protection provided by the R21 vaccine. The researchers also noted that there are other malaria mAbs now in early stages of development that are less likely to interfere with R21.
"The L9LS monoclonal antibody is one of the most exciting malaria interventions now in development, and that makes it all the more important to evaluate interactions with other tools now in use," said ASTMH President Terrie Taylor, a malaria researcher with extensive field experience in Malawi. "The potential interference with R21 is a crucial outcome to consider, though, because of its demonstrated efficacy.
"Overall, the study is a reminder that blazing a trail for a scientific breakthrough rarely involves a straight pathway to success. It highlights why we should value scientists who are committed to thoroughly exploring innovations targeting malaria mortality from one end of the lifespan to the other."

candidato.titulo: Study reveals hidden evolutionary diversity in endangered white pines
candidato.resumo: Accurate species delimitation is fundamental to biodiversity conservation, yet it remains a persistent challenge in species-rich plant groups, particularly conifers, where convergent evolution, gene flow and incomplete lineage sorting often obscure species boundaries.

texto_fonte:
Study reveals hidden evolutionary diversity in endangered white pines
Accurate species delimitation is fundamental to biodiversity conservation, yet it remains a persistent challenge in species-rich plant groups, particularly conifers, where convergent evolution, gene flow and incomplete lineage sorting often obscure species boundaries.
A research team led by professor Wang Xiaoquan from the Institute of Botany of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has revealed the phylogenetic relationships and genomic vulnerability of the Pinus kwangtungensis complex, a group of endangered white pines distributed in subtropical China and Vietnam.
The study was published in Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution on Nov. 10.
The Pinus kwangtungensis complex comprises three nominal species: P. kwangtungensis, P. wangii and P. dalatensis. The complex is mainly distributed in subtropical China and Vietnam, where its habitats are highly fragmented and many populations are confined to isolated limestone mountaintops. P. wangii and P. kwangtungensis are listed as Class I and Class II nationally protected wild plants in China, respectively.
To address these challenges, the research team conducted transcriptome sequencing of 138 individuals from 20 populations covering the entire distribution range of the complex. Using a large number of SNP loci screened from population transcriptomes, together with a unique combination of cytoplasmic DNA markers in Pinaceae (paternally inherited chloroplast genes and maternally inherited mitochondrial genes), they reconstructed the evolutionary relationships among the lineages, assessed genomic vulnerability and established conservation units.
Unexpectedly, the study found that the boundaries of the three nominal species in the complex were all incorrectly defined. Instead, the complex should be divided into three genetic lineages: EAST, WEST and PDAL.
The EAST lineage includes the eastern populations of P. kwangtungensis. The WEST lineage comprises populations traditionally recognized as P. wangii and the western populations of P. kwangtungensis. The PDAL lineage consists of the Hainan Island population of P. kwangtungensis and P. dalatensis and was formed through hybridization between the EAST and WEST lineages.
Notably, adjacent populations of the EAST and WEST lineages show no obvious morphological differences, yet have undergone significant genetic differentiation. This suggests that species boundaries defined solely by morphological characteristics can be obscured by convergent evolution, introgressive hybridization or incomplete lineage sorting. The high genetic differentiation among the three lineages suggests that the evolutionary diversity of this complex has been significantly underestimated.
Population history modeling suggests that the EAST and WEST lineages diverged during the middle Miocene (approximately 15.64 Ma), possibly in response to the strengthening of the East Asian monsoon and regional tectonic uplift. Furthermore, about 68,000 years ago, during the late Pleistocene, the EAST and WEST lineages came into secondary contact and hybridized to form the PDAL lineage. Repeated land bridge connections during the late Pleistocene may have facilitated the dispersal of the PDAL lineage to Hainan Island and Vietnam.
The study further assessed the genomic vulnerability of different populations under future climate scenarios. Model predictions indicate that populations at the western edge of the distribution range, on Hainan Island and in Dalat, Vietnam, are particularly vulnerable under these scenarios.
The researchers recommend that, for the conservation of the P. kwangtungensis complex, the EAST and WEST lineages should be treated as two independent evolutionarily significant units (ESUs), while the Hainan Island population of the PDAL lineage should be managed as a separate management unit, with particular attention to the high-risk populations mentioned above.
Traditional conservation practices often use nominal species as conservation units. This study not only deepens our understanding of the evolutionary history of the P. kwangtungensis complex but also emphasizes the critical role of accurate species delimitation in effective biodiversity conservation.
Under the combined effects of gene flow, hybridization and climate change, biodiversity conservation urgently needs to shift from a "nominal species" approach to an "evolutionary lineage"–oriented framework, enabling more accurate identification of conservation units, assessment of genetic risks and development of differentiated conservation strategies.
Publication details
Chang Liu et al., Reticulate evolution and complex biogeographic history lead to the difficulty in defining conservation units: A case study on Pinus kwangtungensis and its close relatives, Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution (2027). DOI: 10.1016/j.ympev.2026.108776

Video Friday is your weekly selection of awesome robotics videos, collected by your friends at IEEE Spectrum robotics. We also post a weekly calendar of upcoming robotics events for the next few months. Please send us your events for inclusion.
Humanoids 2026: 6–9 December 2026, SANTA CLARA, CA
Enjoy today’s videos!
Drones navigating cluttered spaces often encounter openings narrower than their bodies. We present a design method that jointly optimizes a quadrotor’s geometry and how its two side arms bend on contact. The resulting prototype folds from 31.3 cm to 14.1 cm wide on contact and flies through a 15 cm opening.
[ Paper ] via [ Autonomous Robots Lab ]
Thanks, Kostas!
TeCoBots are soft, snake-like robots that can work alone and can also grab onto each other to form chains, loops and branches, building a new body for each task. A single robot can inch like a worm, roll across gravel and grass, climb inside a pipe and lift a 2.5-liter water bottle. The claw it uses to grab objects is the same one it uses to grab another robot, so linking up needs no extra docking hardware. Linked together, the robots do things none can do alone.
[ TeCoBots ]
Thanks, Mahmud!
AHEADance is a humanoid robot that makes up its dance as the music plays. It listens to the song as it streams in, takes a guess at what the next half second of music will sound like, and moves to match, in the style of whatever is playing. When the music stops, it stands still and waits, and when the music comes back, so does the dancing. Curious what it would do with your favourite song? Play it through the live demo on our project page and watch the robot have a go.
[ AHEADance ]
Thanks, Chengxu!
I am... Not at all sure how I feel about this.
[ Arc Lab ]
Most affordable dexterous hands use tendons, and anyone who has worked with them knows the pain of re-tensioning and replacing them. I wanted to see whether rigid linkages could get you human-like dexterity without that maintenance, and so far the answer looks like yes. Each finger has three actuated degrees of freedom, the hand can grasp and manipulate a wide range of objects, and the whole thing is 3D-printed for less than $650 in parts.
[ PHD‑Hand ]
Thanks, Neel!
I’m not sure that this is an entirely faithful representation of the capabilities of this robot goose, but it’s so cute that we’ll let it slide. For now.
[ Robot Works ]
You’ve seen data-collection gloves. You’ve seen teleoperation gloves. But this is different. What if the glove itself IS the robot hand?
[ TriMI ]
Can we treat a flapping wing like a rotary wing? In our latest IEEE [Robotics and Automation Letters] work, we developed CROBAT, a fully actuated quad-thopter with wing thrust vectoring, enabling independent position and attitude control. The robot demonstrates full-pose flapping flight and tilted perching, showing a pathway toward flapping-wing robots that go beyond navigation toward physical interaction.
[ Paper ]
One robot can work. Two robots can team up. Meet CoMind—Be My Eye, the first framework for proactive, task-aware context sharing in multi-robot collaboration. Robots share selected task context with each other, proactively and in real time. Shared vision is no longer science fiction.
[ Astribot ]
Today Spot is working with people and for people to make our jobs and our communities safer, more reliable, and more intelligent. See what tomorrow brings.
Ugh ouch Atlas don’t DO that.
[ Boston Dynamics ]
Fraunhofer IPA has been doing humanoid robot research since before humanoid robots were cool.
[ Fraunhofer IPA ]
LIMO ULTRA is AgileX Robotics’ newest embodied AI robot development platform for robotics education, research, and hands-on development.
[ AgileX ]
In 2022, an AI drone beat world-champion pilots in head-to-head races. No human at the controls. This is the story behind that breakthrough. This 25-minute documentary takes you behind the scenes of SWIFT, the autonomous racing drone developed by the Robotics and Perception Group at the University of Zurich. Meet the researchers and champion pilots, follow the preparations, and watch human skill face artificial intelligence on the race track.
This Carnegie Mellon University Robotics Institute seminar is from Ben Burchfiel, Co-Founder & CTO at Walden Robotics, on “Learning in Production: Building Physical AI at Walden Robotics.”
Walden Robotics is a full-stack company building both the hardware and physical AI for general-purpose manufacturing robots. Walden was founded in January 2026 and deployed its first robot into production manufacturing two months later. It’s still there and the fleet has been learning on the job ever since. Our core conviction is that the best physical AI will be built via a continuous cycle of deployment and learning grounded in real work. I’ll share lessons from the frontier of end-to-end learning in production manufacturing and why we believe physical AI has reached an inflection point.
[ CMU RI ]

candidato.titulo: Google Donates Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF to Secure AI Agents at Scale
candidato.resumo: Google has announced it is donating Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), placing two important components of its AI agent infrastructure under vendor-neutral open-source governance. By Craig Risi

texto_fonte:
Google has announced it is donating Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), placing two important components of its AI agent infrastructure under vendor-neutral open-source governance. The move is intended to address two emerging challenges in running autonomous agents at scale: securely executing untrusted, AI-generated code and managing the substantial compute overhead created by agents that frequently pause and resume.
The announcement also includes OpenRL, Google's open-source reinforcement learning orchestration project. Together, the projects target different layers of agent infrastructure, from isolated code execution to managing agent lifecycles and coordinating large-scale training workloads. The goal is to establish an open foundation for agentic applications, much as Kubernetes helped standardise container orchestration.
Google argues that conventional Kubernetes workloads and AI agents have fundamentally different execution patterns.
A traditional application typically starts, serves requests, and continues running. An AI agent, however, may execute a tool or code for a few seconds before waiting for model inference, an external API, or human approval. Google estimates that agents can spend 90-95% of their time idle while still holding important state, including memory, files, repositories, and active sessions.
Keeping every agent in a dedicated Pod wastes resources, while scaling to zero introduces delays when environments must be reconstructed. At the other extreme, large-scale agent evaluations can overwhelm Kubernetes control planes when thousands of short-lived execution environments are repeatedly created and destroyed.
Google developed Agent Substrate to address these limitations by separating agent state (actors) from the compute resources (workers) used to execute it.
Actors represent individual agent sessions and retain their state, including filesystem contents, memory, and execution context. Workers provide reusable, pre-warmed execution environments drawn from shared Kubernetes pools.
When an agent needs to resume, Substrate assigns it to an available Worker and restores its previous state. When the agent becomes idle, its state can be saved and the underlying compute resource released.
According to Google, this approach lets agents resume in under 500 milliseconds without creating a new Kubernetes Pod for every execution. It also reduces pressure on the Kubernetes control plane by managing agent lifecycles independently of individual Pod objects.
The second major challenge is security. AI agents routinely execute generated shell commands, install packages, and interact with external tools. Treating this code as trusted creates significant risks, particularly when multiple agents share infrastructure.
Google's gVisor provides an additional isolation boundary through a user-space application kernel. Instead of letting containerised applications interact directly with the host Linux kernel, gVisor intercepts system calls and handles them within its own isolated environment.
This reduces the exposure of the underlying host while retaining much of the efficiency associated with container-based execution.
Agent Substrate also supports Cloud Hypervisor microVMs for workloads requiring hardware-level virtualisation. This gives platform teams flexibility to select an appropriate isolation boundary without changing the overall agent lifecycle model.
The announcement reflects a broader shift in cloud-native infrastructure. Kubernetes was designed around long-running applications and relatively stable workloads. Agentic systems introduce more dynamic execution patterns, where environments must be created, suspended, restored, and isolated at much greater frequency.
Other providers are addressing similar challenges through technologies such as Kata Containers, Firecracker, and dedicated sandboxing platforms. Google's contribution is to combine secure execution with an agent-aware orchestration model and place the resulting technologies within an open ecosystem.
The wider implication is that AI agents need more than an orchestration framework and access to tools; they need their own secure, stateful, and efficiently managed execution infrastructure. By donating these projects to the CNCF, Google is helping establish the foundations for that next layer of cloud-native computing.

candidato.titulo: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved 167-year-old math problem with Claude
candidato.resumo: An anthropic mathematician claims to have solved the Riemann hypothesis using Claude.

texto_fonte:
In the same week that Anthropic was floated on the Nasdaq in its initial public offering, a mathematician employed by the company claims to have discovered proof behind one of the world's most famous math problem, the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis. Levent Alpöge wrote in a paper this week, "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis."
As you're no doubt already aware, and as Alpöge explains, the Riemann Hypothesis is the classic problem in number theory and one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics. Proposed in 1859 by Bernhard Riemann, who gave the problem its name, it is the theory that prime numbers are not in fact random but determined. "The Riemann hypothesis asserts that all interesting solutions of the equation ζ(s) = 0 lie on a certain vertical straight line," the Clay Mathematics Institute explains. "This has been checked for the first 10,000,000,000,000 solutions. A proof that it is true for every interesting solution would shed light on many of the mysteries surrounding the distribution of prime numbers."
As Scientific American notes, the problem is the "North Star for the entire field of number theory, and the most famous open problem in math." Furthermore, the problem was previously thought so insurmountable that experts didn't even bother working on it.
Alpöge not only believes that he has used Claude to discover a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, but also believes the method could easily extend to the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and the Extended Riemann Hypothesis, too. "An astounding amount of mathematics is present in the argument, far more than I had imagined would be necessary as a student," he writes.
This would not be the first time that AI has made a significant discovery or finding in a major STEM field. Earlier this year, OpenAI helped create a breakthrough solution for the Navier-Stokes problem, a finding somewhat overshadowed by a plagiarism controversy.
Alpöge's statement is not without reservation. Aside from confirming whether Claude has actually helped crack the Riemann Hypothesis, which will take some time, he admits sadness at the finding. "It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater."
"In a time of revolution in mathematics, I hope the argument provides a glimpse towards the miracles that lie ahead," Alpöge adds.

candidato.titulo: A star's last gasps: ALMA reveals a giant gas ring and budding hourglass around a star in transition
candidato.resumo: Stars like our sun don't die quietly. In their final act, they swell into red giants, shed their outer layers into space and leave behind a glowing, often strikingly sculpted cloud of gas called a planetary nebula. That transformation is thought to take only a few thousand years, a blink in the life of a star, so catching one in the act is rare.

texto_fonte:
A star's last gasps: ALMA reveals a giant gas ring and budding hourglass around a star in transition
Stars like our sun don't die quietly. In their final act, they swell into red giants, shed their outer layers into space and leave behind a glowing, often strikingly sculpted cloud of gas called a planetary nebula. That transformation is thought to take only a few thousand years, a blink in the life of a star, so catching one in the act is rare.
Using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), a team led by astronomers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory has done just that. Their new images of a star called IRAS 06530-0213, about 12,000 light-years away in the constellation Monoceros, reveal a giant ring of gas that appears to be a frozen fossil of the star's last thermonuclear flare-up, encircling an hourglass-shaped nebula that is only now taking shape.
"Most of us think of stars as unchanging points of light, but this is a real-time snapshot of a star's death throes," said Raghvendra Sahai, senior research scientist at JPL and lead author of the study that has been published in The Astrophysical Journal. "It's the brief, violent transition between a bloated red giant and a glowing planetary nebula, frozen mid-action."
A heartbeat frozen in gas
Late in life, a star like this one burns hydrogen and helium in shells around its core. Every so often, that helium shell flares up in what astronomers call a thermal pulse, a brief burst of nuclear burning that jolts the star and flings material into space. Theorists have long predicted that such pulses leave behind shells of gas, and similar shells have been spotted around other aging stars. But no one had seen one around a star that had already begun its final transformation.
In IRAS 06530, ALMA found a thin, spherical shell of gas that looks like a ring about half a light-year across in the sky. Measuring how fast the gas is moving outward, the team estimates the shell was blown off about 6,500 years ago. This is the first direct evidence of the last thermal pulse before a star of this type enters its final phase, the team says.
"It's essentially a physical snapshot of an event that, until now, we've mostly inferred from theoretical models," said Sahai. "We've caught, for the first time, a star's final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas."
A star in the middle of a dramatic transition
The new images tell the story of what came next. After the pulse, the star's mass loss dropped off for roughly 2,000 years. Then over the next ~1,000 years, mass loss rose sharply again, with the star shedding a thick, lumpy shell of gas, now seen as a tangle of curved filaments surrounding the star.
Inside that, the star has begun to carve out a bipolar (hourglass-shaped) nebula and a dense doughnut of gas around its middle. By the team's estimate, these youngest structures formed within just the last 700 years or so, which means the star crossed over from its red-giant phase very recently, in astronomical terms.
The star's final tens of thousands of years of mass loss have also left a fingerprint: the curved filaments appear to form part of a spiral pattern. Spirals like this are usually attributed to an unseen companion star orbiting the dying one, a stellar dance partner stirring the outflowing gas as it goes.
Strange chemistry, and a missing disk
Two results complicate the picture. First, the gas has an unusual isotopic fingerprint. Isotopes are versions of an element with slightly different weights. In the dense gas near the star, the team found more than expected of the rare, heavy forms of carbon, oxygen and nitrogen. This pattern doesn't match standard models of how stars like this make and mix their elements. Similar fingerprints have been seen in a few other odd objects, and some researchers have proposed that bursts of explosive nuclear burning might be responsible.
Second, the astronomers did not find what they expected near the star. Other dying stars known to have companions typically sit inside a compact disk of dust, like a miniature version of the disks that form planets. Such disks are indirect evidence of ongoing mass transfer/accretion from a close companion, which is the mechanism usually invoked to explain jet-sculpted hourglass shapes.
ALMA sees no such disk around IRAS 06530. Any disk there would be more than 50 times fainter than those seen around well-known cases such as the Red Rectangle. One possibility is that a disk existed briefly, powered a short burst of high-speed jets that helped sculpt the hourglass and then faded away.
"Dying stars so often have hidden companions that reshape their ejected material into intricate, bipolar or multipolar forms instead of simple spheres," said Sahai. "IRAS 06530 shows that the story is more complicated than the tidy explanation we've been using."
Publication details
Raghvendra Sahai et al., The Last Gasps of a Dying Star: ALMA Observations of the Preplanetary Nebula IRAS 06530–0213, The Astrophysical Journal (2026). DOI: 10.3847/1538-4357/aeab9a

candidato.titulo: 10-Member Team Drawn from Chinese Institutions Wins 2026 Gordon Bell Prize
candidato.resumo: Insider Brief PRESS RELEASE — ACM, the Association for Computing Machinery, named a ten-member team drawn from Chinese institutions as the winner of the 2026 ACM Gordon Bell Prize for their project “Closing the FeMo-Cofactor ‘Quantum-Advantage’ Gap with Exascale Supercomputers.” The ACM Gordon Bell Prize tracks the progress of parallel computing and rewards innovation in […]

texto_fonte:
Insider Brief
- A 10-member team from Chinese institutions won the 2026 ACM Gordon Bell Prize for developing the first classical solution at exascale to a simulation problem involving a key component of nitrogen fixation.
- The team modeled the electronic behavior of the iron-molybdenum cofactor, which helps an enzyme convert nitrogen into ammonia.
- The researchers tuned their code for two Chinese supercomputers and achieved a sustained 1.456 exaflops in double precision across 20,480 computing nodes on LineShine.
PRESS RELEASE — ACM, the Association for Computing Machinery, named a ten-member team drawn from Chinese institutions as the winner of the 2026 ACM Gordon Bell Prize for their project “Closing the FeMo-Cofactor ‘Quantum-Advantage’ Gap with Exascale Supercomputers.” The ACM Gordon Bell Prize tracks the progress of parallel computing and rewards innovation in applying high-performance computing to challenges in science, engineering, and large-scale data analytics.
In biochemistry, FeMo refers to the process by which nitrogen is converted into ammonia, a necessity for the growth of plants and other organisms. The effort to understand the intricate structure and function of this process is often called the FeMo Cofactor (FeMoco) CAS problem.
One way scientists have tried to tackle this challenge is by using high-performance computers to simulate the extremely complex interactions that make FeMo possible, including the interplay of atoms, molecules, and electronic states at the quantum level. It is believed that these simulations will yield insights that will benefit many other disciplines, including agriculture and medicine.
This year’s Gordon Bell Prize-winning team is recognized for developing the first “exascale” classical solution to the FeMoco CAS problem. Exascale computers, the world’s most powerful supercomputers, can perform up to a quintillion (a billion billion) calculations per second.
In the abstract of their paper, the team outlines the technical details of their achievement: “The resulting code has been tuned for two exascale supercomputers, LineShine and China’s New-generation Intelligent Super-computer (CNIS), reaching sustained performance on 20,480 LineShine nodes of 1.456 EFLOP/s in double precision (58.9% of the machine peak) and 5.626 EFLOP/s in mixed precision.”
The members of the ACM Gordon Bell Prize-Winning team are Honghui Shang, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei; Zhiya Xiao, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing; Zhuozhao Xia, Hao Wu, and Huan Ma (all of University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei); Yongqing Chen and Bin Li (both of the National High Performance Computer Engineering Technology Research Center, Beijing); Zhenyu Li and Yutong Lu (both of Sun Yat-Sen University, Shenzhen); and Jinlong Yang, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei.
The ACM Gordon Bell Prize was presented today during the International Conference for High-Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis (SC26) in Chicago, Illinois.

candidato.titulo: MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ review: RTX Spark power comes to Windows on Arm desktops, but there are trade-offs
candidato.resumo: MSI's EdgeMesa N AI+ brings Nvidia RTX Spark N1X power to a Windows-on-Arm mini PC with 128GB of unified memory, strong local AI performance, and the ability to game on the side. But its high $7,499 price isn't that much cheaper than more versatile DGX Spark systems.

texto_fonte:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
MSI's EdgeMesa N AI+ mini PC brings Nvidia RTX Spark power to a Windows on Arm desktop. It offers broad app compatibility and the same strong local AI performance we've come to expect from Nvidia's GB10 SoC, but it's still very expensive and less expandable than DGX Spark systems.
Reasons to buy
- + Solid local AI performance for LLMs and image generation, as expected
- + Familiar Windows 11 user experience and app compatibility
- + Can game in a pinch
Reasons to avoid
- - Eye-poppingly expensive
- - Could use more peripheral I/O and smarter port placement
- - Loses the DGX Spark's clustering capability
- - Getting the best gaming performance requires patience
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform, powered by the RTX Spark N1X SoC, passed its most difficult test yet last month at the heart of Windows on Arm laptops. Now we get to see how that chip serves as a Windows on Arm foundation for compact desktops.
We’ve got our hands on the MSI EdgeMesa N AI+, a $7,500 RTX Spark mini PC that gives Windows-native creators and local AI trailblazers access to the same powerful 6144-core Blackwell GPU and 20-core Arm CPU that we recently put to the test in the Surface Laptop Ultra, along with a 128GB pool of unified memory and 4TB of storage in our tested config.
We’ve been testing Nvidia GB10-powered desktop systems for almost a year now in the form of the DGX Spark and friends, and the EdgeMesa N AI+’s design is typical of the breed. It’s wrapped in a slightly hollow-feeling matte aluminum shell with shiny diamond-cut edges and a white plastic back plate.
The design and build quality of this system is a tad underwhelming for the price. It feels nice enough, but It’s hardly a precision-milled statement piece for your desk like a Mac Mini or Mac Studio.
The EdgeMesa draws cool air in through its perforated front panel, which then passes through a dual-fan heatsink with a vapor-chamber base and exhausts through the back panel. The rounded rectangle on the top half of the front panel might look like an optical drive tray, but it’s a purely cosmetic accent.
Around back, the EdgeMesa comes equipped with a 10 Gigabit Ethernet jack, an HDMI 2.1 port, and three USB Type-C 20 Gbps ports with DisplayPort Alt Mode support. A fourth USB-C port is dedicated to the system’s 240 W USB-PD power adapter. The EdgeMesa also has Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 radios inside.
Even with a wireless keyboard and mouse, three 20Gbps USB-C ports feel a bit skimpy as the sole expansion options on a $7,499 PC that’s positioned as a do-it-all desktop for content creation and gaming. If you need to connect multiple monitors to an RTX Spark via USB-C, those scant options for peripheral connectivity shrink even further.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
For comparison, a similarly priced Mac Studio gives you four 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5 ports around back and two more USB Type-C ports, plus an SD card reader, up front. The Mac even provides a headphone jack, while the EdgeMesa requires you to plug in a USB headset or DAC or pair Bluetooth earbuds for audio output.
Even the Mac Mini gives you three Thunderbolt ports out back and two USB 3 10Gbps ports out front.
In use, the tightly spaced, rear-mounted USB-C ports make for an annoying time when doing frequent unplugging and replugging of devices like card readers and external SSDs that are typical in creative workflows. Even one front-panel USB-C port would have made a huge difference in the ease of use of this design.
The EdgeMesa also drops the handy ConnectX RDMA NIC that lets you cluster DGX Spark systems together to run larger AI models. That omission raises a weighty question: is Windows support and application compatibility important enough to trade away any chance of expanding your local AI foundation in the future?
Having tested DGX Sparks for some time now, I’m not sure that’s a wise trade-off, given that most anybody reading this already has a capable Windows PC or Mac that can link up with a DGX Spark for many local AI compute jobs using the Nvidia Sync app.
DGX Spark prices are rising, but you can get MSI's own EdgeXpert with 128GB of memory and a 4TB SSD on sale for $8,099 right now (or $8,499 at full price). Even a $1000 difference in price for that ConnectX NIC in this rarefied air of PC pricing would give me pause if I'm seriously considering how to add local AI capacity to my home.
If you have no inclination whatsoever to learn Linux or networking concepts and just want a no-questions-asked, AI-capable Windows mini PC that can serve as your primary desktop, an RTX Spark system like this may be the way to go. But you'll want to be really sure of your decision before dropping this much cash.
CPU and local AI performance
The performance of the Nvidia GB10 SoC's CPU and GPU resources, whether under DGX OS or Windows, is well-trodden ground by this point. But for a fresh point of comparison, we grabbed AMD’s Ryzen AI Halo, swapped in a spare SSD, and installed Windows 11 Pro, as the Ryzen AI Halo is the only other Windows-ready platform with a large unified memory pool for AI adventurers.
In the Geekbench 7 CPU benchmark under Windows, the Ryzen AI Halo delivers a slightly higher single-threaded score than the MSI EdgeMesa’s RTX Spark Superchip, but its multithreaded score trails the Nvidia part. Using Linux, we would expect both scores to be higher for the Ryzen CPU. But the broader point remains the same: you can expect similar performance from both of these CPUs under Windows.
We’ve left Apple’s Mac Studio with M4 Max in these charts just to emphasize the large performance lead Apple Silicon holds in this benchmark, even with older chips. The current M5 Max would likely open an even larger lead.
In the AgentPerf-Local AI inference benchmark, the MSI EdgeMesa delivered performance practically identical to Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra when running the same Qwen 3.8 27B model with DFlash2 speculative decoding. Its desktop form factor doesn’t seem to give it any extra performance headroom, at least for this LLM serving configuration. Other workloads or models could reveal a difference.
We already tested the RTX Spark against the Ryzen AI Halo in AgentPerf-Local in our Surface Laptop Ultra review, and AMD’s platform ended up way behind GB10 in those tests. And in this new round of testing, AMD's LLM performance is worse under Windows with the Vulkan backend than in Linux with ROCm, taking a whopping four times as long as the EdgeMesa to complete the benchmark.
Strix Halo might have been an appealing local inference option when it was the only open and relatively hackable unified memory platform around, but if you’re serious about local AI performance (and especially if tokens equal dollars for you), a GB10 system is the superior choice in late 2026.
Gaming performance and the tuning experience
Gaming on RTX Spark continues to be a bit of a weird time, and the MSI EdgeMesa N doesn’t change that experience, even with a more generous power and thermal budget than the Surface Laptop Ultra I've already tested.
This platform just doesn’t respond to tuning as we might expect from our experience with traditional gaming PCs and laptops. That weirdness stems, in part, from the imbalance between memory bandwidth and compute resources on GB10.
The 48 SMs of the RTX Spark N1X GPU have to share just 273 GB/s of LPDDR5X bandwidth with the CPU. Compare that with the 672 GB/s of dedicated bandwidth the similarly-specced RTX 5070 enjoys from its 12 GB of GDDR7.
Architectural decisions aside, the RTX Spark platform's gaming performance isn't helped by the fact that full GPU utilization is seemingly hampered by the overhead of Prism x86 emulation in most games. Few (if any) major titles have Arm ports, so this is just a fact of life for the foreseeable future if you buy one of these systems.
Let's see how this all plays out in practice for the RTX Spark versus the Radeon 8060S on board AMD's Strix Halo.
In the 3DMark Steel Nomad raster benchmark, the RTX Spark holds a wide lead over the Ryzen AI Halo, delivering a roughly 56% higher score. That result would suggest a knockout in games for Nvidia’s platform.
But Steel Nomad isn’t representative of real-world gaming performance on the RTX Spark. If we fire up Control Resonant on both platforms and choose the High raster preset at 1440p with Performance upscaling (a 1280x720 input resolution), the RTX Spark and Strix Halo end up a lot closer.
Notably, though, the RTX Spark desktop delivers considerably worse 1% low FPS performance than the Ryzen AI Halo, and this does manifest as visible stutter and hitching. So it's not a clear win for the Nvidia platform.
AMD fans might take heart in the fact that Strix Halo can get this close to the RTX Spark on this raster gaming baseline, but the Radeon 8060S doesn’t have nearly as many tricks up its sleeve to further juice performance.
For one, the quality of FSR 4 upscaling at lower input resolutions on RDNA 3.5 is still not up to par with what you can get out of DLSS 4.5. For two, the Radeon 8060S’s RDNA 3.5 CUs don't match up well against the Spark's Blackwell-powered RT chops.
And FSR Frame Generation is still limited to a doubling of a base frame rate, so you can’t smooth out gameplay on a high-refresh-rate monitor nearly as well as you can with DLSS MFG.
So even if their raster baseline frame rates are similar, the Radeon 8060S isn't delivering the same image quality in Control Resonant as an RTX Spark system does with all its DLSS features in play.
RT is the next step for squeezing better image quality out of Control Resonant. Surprisingly, enabling RT Medium only results in a 14% performance hit on the Spark versus 38% on the AI Halo. That might be due in part to the efficiency of DLSS Ray Reconstruction versus the Northlight engine's built-in denoiser, but the RT prowess of Blackwell certainly can't hurt.
A 52.3 FPS average with a 75 ms average PC latency is an OK baseline — at least in the context of an RTX Spark system — for adding MFG to the mix for a smoother experience, especially since Control Resonant seems to link Nvidia Reflex latency reduction to that tech anyway. But dialing in MFG 3X with the default MFG Preset B model still results in a PC latency of 96 ms on average, which is too high to be enjoyable, even if we give the Spark some slack.
I found that the new MFG Preset C, available through the Nvidia App, significantly lowered latency versus the more compute-intensive Preset B. While input latency with Preset C is still high at about 84 ms, we have to take every bit of help we can get here, and the resulting 145 FPS average is notably smoother than native gameplay on my 160 Hz monitor.
We only had time to dive into this one title in our testing, but when Nvidia says the RTX Spark platform is great for 1440p gaming, our experience suggests that you need to be ready to tweak DLSS upscaling and dial in MFG for more demanding games. And look: that’s fine. These are proven technologies at this point, and they let us get a better experience out of this platform than native rendering would allow.
But all of these data points should go to show that if you're used to the low input latency and predictable performance scaling characteristics of an x86 desktop gaming PC with a discrete GPU, the RTX Spark platform still has a ways to go before it can truly replace such a system.
Power draw and noise levels
During our AgentPerf-Local LLM benchmark, the EdgeMesa N AI+ pulls about 140 W from the wall, and under that load, it produces just 38.2 dBA at 18” (46 cm) according to our calibrated SPL meter, well below the 47.4 dBA of the RTX Spark-powered Surface Laptop Ultra and the 48 dBA of the Ryzen AI Halo.
That makes the EdgeMesa an easy system to live with for local AI work, especially if it’s moonlighting as an AI inference server or always-on agent host in shared spaces.
Under gaming workloads, the EdgeMesa draws about 200 W. With more heat to dissipate, the MSI box’s noise output rises to 40.7 dBA, which is still much quieter than the average gaming laptop and will easily be covered by speakers or a closed-back gaming headset.
The Ryzen AI Halo, on the other hand, emits a piercing 46.9 dBA whine while gaming, much closer to what we expect from a gaming laptop. And that’s not because it has that much more heat to dissipate; the AI Halo is pulling about 209 W with Control Resonant running.
Under that same load, the EdgeMesa’s fans have a slightly high-pitched character to them, but it’s much less pronounced than the typical gaming laptop. Mostly, the sound from the system is that of air moving, and it's easy to ignore (so much so that I missed the aural cues I sometimes listen for when a benchmark finishes).
MSI deserves high praise for this system’s thermal design and cooling system. It’s both quiet and pleasant-sounding, and those factors aren’t always a given with mini PCs.
Bottom line
If you’re a hardcore Windows fan who’s been intrigued by Nvidia’s DGX Sparks for local AI, but you've been repelled by the idea of using Linux, RTX Spark desktops like this MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ finally pair your preferred OS with the same 6144-core Nvidia Blackwell GPU, 20-core Arm CPU, and up to 128GB of unified memory that give those systems their local AI grunt.
These systems are a potentially exciting prospect for those who want to explore the possibilities of local AI and agentic workflows without the privacy and token caps of cloud models, all from the comfort of Windows.
But that potential comes with tradeoffs that you’ll need to weigh carefully before buying. And at an eye-popping $7,499 for the 128GB EdgeMesa configuration with a 4TB SSD that we tested, those tradeoffs weigh all the more heavily.
The MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ delivers essentially the same performance from the RTX Spark N1X SoC (aka GB10) we’ve come to know and love for about a year now. It’s reasonably fast for local LLM inference, and it offers leading performance with generative AI workflows like images and videos in ComfyUI. Its Arm CPU offers solid enough single-threaded and multi-threaded performance for general computing tasks, and it can game in a pinch. The EdgeMesa is laudably quiet, too — no small feat for a compact PC like this.
But in exchange for Windows support, RTX Spark desktops lose the valuable expandability offered by the ConnectX 7 RDMA NIC that comes standard on DGX Spark boxes. So if you want to try your hand at running a bigger, more intelligent LLM than you can fit in one of these systems’ unified memory pools through clustering, you are forever out of luck if you go down the RTX path.
Even if you can live without the ConnectX NIC, we’re a bit let down by the peripheral connectivity the EdgeMesa N AI+ offers, both for its price and for its ambitions as a do-it-all creator and gaming system.
With just three 20 Gbps USB Type-C ports on the back panel that have to do double duty as display outputs in multi-monitor setups, folks who have to juggle external storage and card readers frequently may find both the number and placement of those ports an obstacle to a smooth workflow. We really would have liked to see more expansion ports on this system overall, or at least one on the front panel.
Nvidia loves to tout the gaming capability of Windows on Arm with RTX Spark systems, but we're still not that impressed by the experience in practice, especially for a system this expensive.
It's nice that you can enjoy PC gaming on these systems at all, but even in a desktop with more power and thermal budget to spare, the gaming performance and responsiveness we saw can only be described as adequate. We were especially surprised by the gulf in 1% low FPS between the RTX Spark and the much cheaper Ryzen AI Halo in Control Resonant, despite the RTX Spark N1X's much stronger GPU on paper.
In general, we find that it takes a lot of careful tweaking and application of DLSS magic to get around this platform's wrinkles for gaming (or a willingness to just let the Nvidia App optimize your game settings). In other words, don't retire your dedicated gaming PC or laptop just yet.
The large memory pools available from RTX Spark systems have uses beyond local AI, of course. Nvidia GPUs are favorites for creative work on Windows, and if you work with massive 3D or game development projects, or you edit lots of high-resolution video, RTX Sparks are the first unified memory systems to pair a powerful Nvidia GPU with this much VRAM for Windows users.
Adobe just updated several of its Creative Suite apps with Arm-native versions, so if you’re trying to blaze the trail of agentic content creation and generation in this modern age, an RTX Spark desktop (or laptop, for that matter) might be intriguing.
But we feel like $7,499 is still a ton of money to spend on a system like this to run Adobe's apps specifically, unless a large unified memory pool is particularly useful for your work today.
All told, we're left scratching our heads a bit about who RTX Spark desktops are really for. RTX Spark laptops meaningfully expanded the capabilities of mobile Windows on Arm systems thanks to the unmatched AI compute resources of their Blackwell GPUs and support for the full Nvidia software stack, along with solid CPU performance and battery life.
But compared to both the existing DGX Spark platform and other mini PCs, RTX Spark desktops like the MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ ask you to give up a lot in exchange for the Nvidia-powered Windows on Arm experience, especially for the high prices they’re likely to command amid the current silicon supply crunch.
If you’re a hardcore Windows-native developer or creator looking to explore the boundaries of what’s possible from local and agentic AI and want the best possible Microsoft-powered foundation for those activities, an RTX Spark desktop might be the right choice for the job, assuming you have the cash.
But if you're just curious, we'd wait for the value proposition of local or agentic AI under Windows to firm up a bit and for the prices of these systems to come down before spending thousands of dollars on a still-fuzzy vision of the future of computing.
As the Senior Analyst, Graphics at Tom's Hardware, Jeff Kampman covers everything that has to do with graphics cards, gaming performance, and more. From integrated graphics processors to discrete graphics cards to the hyperscale installations powering our AI future, if it's got a GPU in it, Jeff is on it.

candidato.titulo: Following the “mathocalypse,” mathematicians consider the future
candidato.resumo: A panel discussion at MIT explored AI’s implications for mathematical discovery and the people who make it their profession.

texto_fonte:
It’s been a tumultuous year for math. Big open questions that have occupied mathematicians for decades are now being solved in a matter of hours by artificial intelligence agents that companies deploy by the thousands to work on a single problem in tireless lockstep.
AI’s relentless rise is raising existential questions for the field: How will the tools affect humans’ understanding of mathematical concepts? In the face of AI’s brute-force productivity, will mathematicians still have jobs? And what will all this mean for mathematics as an intellectual pursuit?
At MIT, mathematicians grappled with these and other questions at a panel discussion on Monday titled “AI and Society: The Future of Math.” Leading mathematicians from MIT, Harvard University, Northwestern University, and New York University — each experts in their respective fields — sat down for a conversation that touched on the quality of AI math, how AI is challenging long-established research norms, and the evolving opportunities for mathematicians, whether they embrace the machines or remain “AI vegans.”
The wide-ranging discussion, which took place in a packed lecture hall in MIT’s Building 3, was moderated by science writer Kevin Hartnett, author of “The Proof in the Code,” and featured Jacopo Borga, the Cecil and Ida Green Career Development Assistant Professor of Mathematics at MIT; Michael Hopkins, the George Putnam Professor of Pure and Applied Mathematics at Harvard University; Bryna Kra, the Sarah Rebecca Roland Professor of Mathematics at Northwestern University; and Tristan Buckmaster, professor of mathematics at New York University's Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences.
As the panelists shared their various and at times conflicting perspectives on AI’s impact, one thing was clear:
“Math has changed more in the last two months than in the last 100 years,” said Kra, who cautioned that AI’s power will change what it is to be a mathematician and what it will take to advance human knowledge in meaningful ways. “It’s like the first sentence in ‘A Tale of Two Cities’: ‘It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.’ It’s a really exciting moment … and also scary.”
AI’s sprint
Artificial intelligence has made steady strides over the last decade thanks in large part to mathematicians themselves, who out of curiosity have been honing AI models to solve problems with known solutions. These early exercises proved successful, most notably in 2025. That summer, at the International Mathematical Olympiad, Google DeepMind’s AI models achieved gold-medal status by quickly finding solutions to most of the problems that were posed to the world’s best high school mathematicians.
Around that same time, other mathematicians found that some AI systems could solve problems with known solutions, but in ways that were slightly improved compared to the solutions that human mathematicians had derived.
In 2026, AI’s power took a quantum leap. In several instances, scientists found that models could solve open-ended research questions — mathematical problems that had no known answer. Then, in September, OpenAI made a field-shaking announcement: The company focused thousands of its AI agents on a singular challenge, and after 88 hours, the agents produced a proof related to the Navier-Stokes equation — a Millienum Prize Problem that is one of seven unsolvable mathematical Holy Grails.
OpenAI’s sudden interest in the Navier-Stokes challenge coincided with work by Tristan Buckmaster, one of the panelists. After a year of progress, he and his collaborator, at rival AI behemoth Anthropic, were on the cusp of solving the problem when OpenAI made its announcement.
OpenAI’s sprint to be first to the proof opened up a huge debate, about whether proper credit was given, whether the mathematicians’ data was leaked, how the AI agents arrived at their solution, whether that solution makes any meaningful sense, and above all, how AI will change mathematical research.
A month later, the company doubled down, releasing 722 manuscripts, organized into categories that ran the gamut of mathematical topics. The manuscripts claimed to have used AI entirely to solve many of math’s major, unsolved problems — an achievement that has widely been coined the “mathocalypse.”
But many mathematicians insist that it isn’t just about whether a problem can be solved, but also, how. And, they say, when they’ve looked into the details of AI proofs, it’s not clear how the agents arrived at their conclusions.
“The papers themselves are nonsense,” Hopkins said during Monday’s discussion, noting that AI-generated proofs contain “strange ideas.” He continued: “There still is a sense of AI math versus human math.”
“For math to be important, it has to have human understanding,” Buckmaster added.
New norms
For mathematicians like Kra, this moment in math’s history presents an opportunity to let go of certain long-held norms of mathematical research, such as competition among research groups and the prestige of being the first to prove an idea, also known as priority.
“It shouldn’t matter that you’re first,” Kra said. “Speed should not be a priority. It’s not about the proof production anymore. We need to find other ways to assess understanding.”
However, “We can throw away priority, but people are going to want to be pioneers,” Hopkins countered, noting the challenge that mathematicians will now face in making in-roads where AI has already clear-cut.
Kra, however, struck a hopeful counterpoint:
“You can be a pioneer in different ways, for instance in communicating [how a proof came to be],” said Kra, who helped this year to draft the Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics — a statement signed by mathematicians around the world that calls for action to address the risks that AI poses to mathematical research. “Communication of math is even more important now.”
Indeed, the panelists have already seen a subtle shift in what is expected of a mathematician, at all levels, from undergraduate students to early and established career mathematicians.
“The interview is becoming more important,” said Kra, noting that it’s no longer enough to accept, hire, or promote a mathematician based on ideas they have written or published — they have to also show that they understand and can explain those ideas to another person.
Human math
AI is also making mathematicians question the role of academic journals, which have long been the benchmark for evaluating and validating mathematical advances.
“Ninety percent of how we’ve judged [mathematicians] are through journals,” says Jacopo Borga, who is an early-career mathematician at MIT. “I’m not sure that’s how we should do this anymore. We should come up with a new metric and let it evolve.”
Kra, who is a managing editor of a specialty journal, is seeing a huge increase in the number of papers submitted, primarily reporting results that were generated or assisted by AI. To deal with the deluge, that particular journal has had to hire an additional managing editor.
Where journal editors have traditionally prioritized publishing new proofs that push the field forward, Kra sees that, in response to AI “slop,” some publications are putting more value on exposition — the section of a paper that explains the reasoning behind a conjecture or proof. For now, humans have the advantage over AI in communicating mathematical ideas.
“There’s a real art to exposition, if you can explain something in a clear and elegant way,” Hopkins echoed.
Kra noted that there are experimental journals coming online now, that are designed to highlight uniquely human contributions to mathematics. For instance, there are journals that publish expositions, such as papers that explain an old result in a new way that modern mathematicians can understand.
“There is a lot of opportunity to curate and translate knowledge,” said Hopkins, who shared that one of his students has been working to prove a theorem from the 1970s. The original language and construction from that decades-old theorem, he said, was just as foreign as some of AI’s proofs today.
In noting novel approaches journals are taking in response to AI, Kra also mentioned Mathematical Discourse, a new peer-reviewed “video journal” that will feature videos of people giving talks about mathematical research. The journal’s preliminary site states that “giving a mathematical talk captures the human side of mathematics in a unique way, and supporting these human aspects of our discipline will be ever more important in the coming years.”
“A new kind of mathematician”
The rise of AI may be hitting especially hard for students, who are still learning the fundamentals in the presence of so many AI shortcuts.
“Mathematics is probably the slowest science you can do,” said Borga, to appreciative laughs from the audience. “Students today are bombarded by [conflicting messages of] what they should do, and are overwhelmed. We need to give them space to learn.”
How they should learn could be a matter of personal belief.
“There is a big faction of my group who are ‘AI vegans’ [people who do not use AI], while others are using it,” said Hopkins, who is finding ways to support both groups.
He also highlighted one particular student, who seemed to be a sort of “horse whisperer of AI.” This student has good mathematical instincts, Hopkins said, but struggles with execution. They are motivated by curiosity, rather than being first to a solution, and have a way of prompting AI to produce interesting insights.
“This may be a new kind of mathematician,” Hopkins said.
As AI forces the field of mathematics to adapt and change its centuries-long ways of pursuing knowledge, Borga and others see the moment as a new beginning, rather than math’s end.
“The castle is collapsing,” Borga says. “There’s open ground to explore.”
“AI is going to affect everyone (beyond mathematicians),” said Buckmaster, who urged students to stay the course “rather than escape or jump ship to another field. … Think of new ways to be creative and communicate your ideas,” he said. “Just do what you love.”
The panel discussion, co-sponsored by the Department of Mathematics, is the first of a planned series hosted by MITHIC and SERC exploring how AI is reshaping our personal and professional lives.

texto_fonte:
Where do ions go? Hidden differences inside next-generation battery materials
When a rechargeable battery operates, ions move into and out of its electrode materials. But where exactly do these ions settle inside the crystal structure? And does their location affect how well a battery performs? These questions are particularly important for next-generation batteries that use abundant elements such as sodium, magnesium and calcium instead of lithium.
A research team at Tohoku University has now revealed that these ions behave very differently, even when inserted into the same electrode material. Their findings show how the locations of individual ions and the structural changes around them can influence battery performance and durability.
"Understanding where ions settle inside an electrode material is essential for designing batteries that can store more energy and last longer," says Hongyi Li, assistant professor at Tohoku University's Institute for Materials Research.
Details of the findings were published in the journal Chemistry of Materials.
Mapping ions inside manganese dioxide
The researchers focused on hollandite-type manganese dioxide (α-MnO₂), a material containing tiny, one-dimensional tunnels within its crystal structure. These tunnels provide pathways for ions to enter and move through the material. However, simply having enough space for ions does not guarantee that they can move easily or that the surrounding crystal structure will remain stable.
To investigate these challenges, the team combined advanced electron microscopy at the Tohoku Center of Excellence for Microscopy (TCEM) at Tohoku University with X-ray absorption spectroscopy at NanoTerasu, a next-generation synchrotron radiation facility. This approach allowed them to examine both the locations of inserted ions and changes in the surrounding atomic structure and electronic states.
Magnesium insertion brings distortion and damage
The differences were striking. Sodium ions spread relatively uniformly throughout the particles and occupied positions near the centers of the tunnels. Magnesium ions also entered the particles but tended to accumulate near their surfaces, occupying positions away from the tunnel centers. This was accompanied by significant distortion of the surrounding crystal structure. Calcium ions, meanwhile, remained mainly near the particle surfaces, with little evidence of insertion into the interior tunnels.
X-ray absorption measurements revealed another important difference: magnesium insertion caused more pronounced changes in the electronic states of manganese near the particle surfaces, whereas sodium produced relatively uniform changes and calcium produced only minor changes.
The researchers also found that repeated magnesium insertion and extraction damaged parts of the tunnel structure near the particle surfaces, even though the overall crystal structure remained largely intact. This local damage was associated with material loss and declining battery capacity.
The findings highlight that designing better battery electrodes requires more than providing pathways for ions. Controlling where ions settle and how they affect the surrounding atoms may be just as important. These insights could help researchers develop more durable, higher-capacity cathode materials for next-generation rechargeable batteries.
Publication details
Hongyi Li et al., Atomic-Scale Origin of Spatially Heterogeneous Insertion in Hollandite-Type MnO2, Chemistry of Materials (2026). DOI: 10.1021/acs.chemmater.6c02510

candidato.titulo: iFood sofre outro vazamento de dados de clientes
candidato.resumo: Telefones, CPFs e informações de parceiros e entregadores também foram expostas. É o segundo caso na plataforma em 2026. iFood sofre outro vazamento de dados de clientes

texto_fonte:
Resumo IA
- O iFood confirmou que dados cadastrais de clientes foram acessados indevidamente, incluindo telefones, CPFs e outras informações.
- O incidente, identificado e contido em 14/11, também afetou representantes de restaurantes, parceiros e entregadores.
- A empresa notificou a ANPD e colaborará com a autoridade.
O iFood confirmou nesta quinta-feira (19/11) que dados cadastrais de clientes foram acessados indevidamente. Segundo a empresa, o incidente foi identificado e contido em 14/11, mas o número de pessoas afetadas não foi divulgado.
De acordo com o iFood, senhas, cartões, outros meios de pagamento, saldos, extratos bancários e informações biométricas não foram acessados. A empresa também afirma que, até o momento, não encontrou evidências de divulgação ou uso indevido desses dados.
Quais dados foram expostos?
As informações acessadas variam. No caso de clientes e usuários do iFood Benefícios, foram expostos apenas números de telefone. Já representantes de restaurantes e parceiros podem ter tido o telefone cadastrado e/ou o CPF acessados.
Entre entregadores, os dados vazados podem incluir nome, e-mail, telefone e CPF. Em alguns casos, também foram acessados números de agência e conta usados para o repasse dos pagamentos.
O iFood deve enviar um e-mail aos afetados com o detalhamento dos dados acessados. A empresa notificou a Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) e afirma colaborar com a autoridade.
Segundo vazamento do iFood em 2026
Em junho, o iFood comunicou outro incidente de segurança, ocorrido em dezembro de 2025, que expôs dados cadastrais de aproximadamente 1,2 milhão de pessoas — cerca de 2% da base de usuários da plataforma.
Na ocasião, foram acessados nomes e CPFs. A empresa afirmou que senhas, meios de pagamento e registros financeiros não foram comprometidos.
